A Goldman Sachs 2026 industry forecast projects a $415 billion global robotaxi market and a $560 billion autonomous-trucking market by 2035. The same research estimates approximately $2 trillion in broader autonomous-vehicle revenue, including hardware, software, and services. It notes that some of that spending would shift from existing transportation activities. These forecasts show the scale of the autonomous-driving opportunity, which extends beyond passenger transport to the technologies covered in 12 Best Autonomous Driving Stocks to Buy at the beginning of 2026.

The research also forecasts that autonomous trucks could become cost-competitive with human-driven trucks in the United States in 2028. It models the higher hardware cost per truck falling from $125,000–150,000 today to $35,000–40,000 by 2035. These remain projections, but they show equipment cost as a measurable driver of the commercial opportunity. 11 Best Robotics Stocks to Buy Right Now examines the broader automation market.

Regulators have opened new routes toward deployment. Britain's Department for Transport opened applications for taxi, bus and private-hire-style self-driving pilots on May 22, 2026. It requires safety assessments. This includes cybersecurity checks and local consent for services. Readers can explore the sector further in 11 Best Self-Driving Car Stocks to Buy According to Analysts.

The UK government's pilot guidance separates operations without a safety driver from supervised trials. It requires a documented safety case and suitable vehicle maintenance and software management procedures. The same guidance also requires insurance covering liabilities from the vehicle and its operation, incident-management protocols and pre-deployment checks. Removing the onboard driver does not remove the operator's responsibility for maintaining the vehicle and managing its operation.

Singapore shows the gap between passenger adoption and revenue since its Land Transport Authority reported more than 11,500 unique riders on Punggol's autonomous shuttles by July 12, 2026. However, its July update said fixed-route rides would stay free while operators prepared service enhancements. Among approximately 270 residents the authority surveyed, almost 60% wanted more choice over where they board and alight, and around 40% preferred more direct routes. The authority outlined an on-demand pilot with more direct routes. Passenger interest alone does not establish paying demand.

Dubai's Roads and Transport Authority reported more than four million robotaxi kilometers and 7,613 passenger trips in its August 19, 2026 update. The fleet totals 144 vehicles, 48 of them in active operation. The authority reiterated its target of making 25% of transportation trips autonomous by 2030, reported 97% customer satisfaction and described a phased rollout through defined operating zones, from safety-driver trials toward fully driverless public transportation.

title: Elon Musk, crypto just placed huge midterm bets, and traders should pay attention

Elon Musk, crypto just placed huge midterm bets, and traders should pay attention
Bibhu Pattnaik
Thu, October 29, 2026 at 3:06 PM EDT 2 min read
COIN
TSLA
DKNG
Explore stocks on Coinbase

With less than a week to go before the Nov. 3 midterm elections, the biggest checks are coming from familiar names in tech and crypto.

Tesla owner Elon Musk has given $446 million to Republican-aligned groups, making him the largest individual donor of the cycle, according to a report by Al Jazeera.

That is nearly three times the $150 million from the next biggest donors, Elizabeth and Richard Uihlein.

Crypto outspends old-school giants

Crypto companies are among the biggest organizational donors. Coinbase has given $57.8 million, Ripple $49.6 million and Foris DAX, the company behind Crypto.com, $39 million.

Together, that is more than $146 million.

Related: Elon Musk has a bold answer to America's $40 trillion debt crisis

Both Coinbase and Ripple gave more than industrial conglomerate Koch, at $46.8 million, and sports betting firm DraftKings, at $40.4 million. However, the outlet did not specify which groups received the crypto firms' money.

The top 50 contributors have spent $2.77 billion in total. Republican-aligned groups received about $1.67 billion, or roughly 60%, while Democratic-aligned groups took in $832 million, about 30%.

The remaining $264 million went to bipartisan or special-interest causes. Ad spending this cycle is projected to reach $11.6 billion, according to AdImpact report shared by Al Jazeera.

Why traders should care

The stakes for crypto are high. The industry's top priority in Washington, the CLARITY Act, which would set out which regulator oversees different digital assets, failed 49–50 in the Senate on Sept. 15.

If Democrats win control of Congress, long-time crypto critics such as Rep. Maxine Waters (D-Calif.) and Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) could gain influence over key financial committees, making new crypto laws harder to pass.

Bitcoin has also struggled after past midterms.

Analyst Ali Charts found Bitcoin fell between 27% and 72% after each of the last four midterms, though he noted the elections didn't necessarily cause those drops.

Bitcoin trades near $81,000, down more than 4% for October.

Millions of Americans have indirect exposure to Elon Musk's business empire through index funds in their 401(k) accounts, even if they have never purchased shares of his companies directly.

A potential merger could change that exposure before the end of the year.

Senior Equity Research Analyst at Barclays, Dan Levy, told clients that Tesla and SpaceX could merge before December 2026, potentially creating one of the largest publicly traded companies by valuation, The Wealth Advisor reported.

The prospect raises questions about how such a deal could affect passive index funds and the retirement savings tied to them.

Tesla is already part of the S&P 500, according to the S&P Dow Jones Indices' SPY/SPX fact sheet, meaning its stock influences many broad-market and target-date funds held in workplace retirement plans. 

If a merger takes SpaceX public, index providers could adjust their holdings, potentially changing millions of Americans' portfolio exposure without requiring them to take any action.

Also read: SpaceX is now in your 401(k), and Musk is the risk

Barclays maps a Tesla-SpaceX share-swap ratio before the December vote

Barclays laid out the share-swap arithmetic for a potential Tesla-SpaceX merger, The Wealth Advisor reported. Based on the analysis, Tesla shareholders could receive about 0.7 SpaceX shares for each Tesla share in an all-stock deal before any acquisition premium.

Barclays indicated the two companies combined would have a market value of roughly $3.6 trillion, with Tesla's December 6, 2026, meeting as the possible approval window.

Each Tesla share would convert into a stake in the combined entity's aerospace, artificial intelligence, and automotive revenue streams, which Barclays framed as a vertical-integration thesis.

Barclay's ownership breakdown helps explain why SpaceX would likely be the acquiring entity in any proposed deal. Musk owns roughly 20% of Tesla and about 48% of SpaceX, but supervoting shares give him approximately 82% of SpaceX's voting power.

Why passive index funds already own more Tesla than most savers realize

Tesla joined the S&P 500 in late 2020 and now accounts for about 2% of the benchmark powering millions of American 401(k) accounts, Quartz reported. 

That weighting means the stock's daily moves ripple directly through target-date funds, total-market funds, and large-cap index funds that dominate workplace retirement menus.

Deliveries got it started

Then the SpaceX talk took over

Key Takeaways

Elon Musk dismissed an estimate that humanoid robots will use about 0.04% of 2026's DRAM output, saying robot memory needs will exceed everything else on Earth.

Robots won't move Micron's results for years, but a big new buyer late in the decade could keep memory scarce just as the Street expects Micron's margins to fade.

Tesla cut the memory on its Optimus robot chips to get enough supply, while memory makers like Micron and SK hynix already can't keep up with AI data centers.

Micron trades at 5.3x forward earnings, less than half its three-year average, so the market is pricing today's earnings as a peak.

Elon Musk thinks the biggest memory buyer on Earth will eventually be robots. That's a big claim for Micron Technology (MU:NASDAQ) and SK hynix (SKHY:NASDAQ), which already can't make memory fast enough for AI data centers.

On Oct. 11, Counterpoint Research projected that DRAM demand from humanoid robots will rise about 20x by 2030. An X user who posts as @zephyr_z9 then ran the numbers: Counterpoint's 2030 figure works out to about 550,000 humanoids a year using 21.5 petabytes of DRAM, or "around 0.04% of 2026 DRAM production."

Musk, whose Tesla (TSLA:NASDAQ) is building the Optimus humanoid, had a two-word answer: "Silly analysis."

"Robot RAM needs will exceed everything else on Earth, as you need the robots to be on physical substates in order to shape atoms," he wrote on X on Oct. 26.

Both sides can be right at once. And for Micron, the timing is what matters.

Small potatoes for years

The 0.04% math holds up. Even if robot production ran 20x higher, about 11 million a year, @zephyr_z9 figures robots would need 430 petabytes of DRAM. That's still under 1% of what the industry will make this year.

Micron's own CEO is pitching the robot future, too. Sanjay Mehrotra said on Micron's fiscal fourth-quarter call on Sept. 30 that "humanoid robots will also require similar amounts of memory and storage as autonomous vehicles." But that's a story for the end of the decade.

The Street's earnings path for Micron runs on data center demand, with normalized EPS expected to more than double to $176.58 in fiscal 2027 and reach $206.89 in fiscal 2028.

title: Tesla vs. Ford: Which Stock Has an Edge After Q3 Earnings?

Tesla vs. Ford: Which Stock Has an Edge After Q3 Earnings?
Rimmi Singhi

F

Trading disclosure

Tesla TSLA and Ford F both topped Wall Street's third-quarter 2026 EPS estimates, but what investors took away from the two reports was quite different. Tesla tackled its biggest overhang by cutting its 2026 capital expenditure plan from $25 billion to $20 billion. Ford tightened its 2026 adjusted EBIT guidance to $10.5 billion-$11 billion, from $10 billion-$11 billion earlier, and said 2027 earnings should be roughly in line with this year's.

Over the past month, Tesla shares have gained 14% while Ford has lost 1%. With third-quarter results now behind us, which stock is better positioned from here?

Zacks Investment Research

Image Source: Zacks Investment Research

The Case for Tesla

Tesla's case rests on improving vehicle demand, healthier auto and energy margins and an AI roadmap with measurable milestones, even as high R&D spending weighs on operating profit.

Tesla's deliveries and order backlog show demand holding up well. The company delivered 486,532 vehicles in its latest reported quarter, its second straight quarter above 480,000 units, and its passenger vehicle order backlog is the highest in four years. Management says demand is running well ahead of production, largely helped by rising FSD adoption. More than 75% of new North American deliveries included a paid FSD subscription at delivery. Recently, Latvia approved FSD, making it the 10th EU country to do so, according to Teslarati.

Gross margins are following volume. Automotive gross margin rose to 18.5% from 17% a year earlier. Energy storage deployments reached 13.7 GWh, up 10% year over year, while energy gross margin climbed to 33.1% from 20.4% in the second quarter of 2026. With CEO Elon Musk saying Megapack supply for 2027 is almost sold out, this business has strong forward visibility.

The AI story now has progress to show. Tesla began deploying Cybercabs in Austin in September 2026, and Musk says the fleet there has grown tenfold in roughly a month. Cumulative unsupervised Robotaxi miles rose eightfold sequentially to nearly 2 million. Management expects Robotaxi to contribute more meaningfully to revenues from next year.

The weak spot is operating profit, which contracted as R&D costs rose. It is expected to keep declining year over year in the coming quarters as Tesla funds its next growth cycle, and supply chain challenges persist. Still, the pressure is investment-led rather than demand-led. With strong demand, recovering gross margins, a return to positive free cash flow and tangible AI milestones, the narrative is getting stronger.

Walmart (NYSE: $WMT), Eli Lilly (NYSE: $LLY), Cigna Group (NYSE: $CI), Carnival (NYSE: $CCL) and Arcos Dorados (NYSE: $ARCO) have objected to plans to offer tokenized versions of their shares on a trading venue backed by crypto exchange OKX and Intercontinental Exchange (NYSE: $ICE).

The five companies were added to OKXICE TSV's list in a notice dated October 28, bringing the number of objecting companies to 38. The total has climbed from nine on October 15, as objections have spread across technology, finance, retail, health care and travel.

The latest additions include Walmart, the world's largest retailer, and Arcos Dorados, the largest McDonald's franchisee in Latin America. Both join companies that have already opposed the listings, including McDonald's (NYSE: $MCD), Microsoft (NASDAQ: $MSFT), JPMorgan Chase (NYSE: $JPM), Coca-Cola (NYSE: $KO) and Dell Technologies (NYSE: $DELL).

More From Cryptoprowl:

Cardano Founder Hoskinson Says Midnight Will Surpass Zcash, Urges Gemini to List ADA

Stacks Founder Warns Bitcoin Security Breach Could Hit Entire Crypto Market

Coinbase Targets Banks As Institutional Crypto Adoption Grows

Crypto Heavyweights Back OKX at $25B Valuation

Eli Lilly and Cigna also add to the health care sector's representation on the list, alongside UnitedHealth Group and Moderna.

The objections have consequences under an exemption introduced by the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC). Under the agency's September order, a venue seeking to offer tokenized shares issued by an unaffiliated third party must notify the company first.

If the company submits a written objection within 30 days, the venue cannot list that tokenized version of its stock under the exemption.

The rule applies to the specific trading venue, and the notices do not explain why the companies objected.

OKXICE TSV is a joint venture between ICE, the parent company of the New York Stock Exchange, and OKX's US holding company. It plans to let approved users trade tokenized US stocks around the clock through permissioned Uniswap (CRYPTO: $UNI) v4 pools on OKX's XLayer blockchain, using stablecoins such as USDC.

The list could grow further, as companies have 30 days after receiving notice to object. Major names including Nvidia (NASDAQ: $NVDA), Tesla (NASDAQ: $TSLA), Apple (NASDAQ: $AAPL) and Amazon (NASDAQ: $AMZN) have not yet objected.

Ford generated adjusted earnings before interest and taxes (EBIT) of $2.7 billion, up 3% year over year. Adjusted EBIT margin expanded 30 basis points to 5.4%, reflecting improved operating efficiency despite lower revenues.

Ford Blue Faces Volume and Commodity Pressures

Ford Blue revenues declined 3% year over year to $27.1 billion as wholesale volumes fell 10% to 657,000 units. Lower sales reflected discontinued models and disruptions associated with the Middle East conflict. Favorable product mix provided a partial offset.

Segment EBIT decreased 10% to $1.39 billion, while EBIT margin contracted to 5.1% from 5.5%. Higher commodity costs also weighed on profitability.

Demand for higher-margin vehicles remained encouraging. Explorer's Tremor and Platinum trims registered nearly 60% year-to-date sales growth in the United States. F-Series achieved the highest retail share among full-size truck brands during the quarter.

F's Model e Loss Narrows Amid EV Restructuring

Ford Model e revenues declined 31% to $1.2 billion, with wholesale volumes falling 31% to 34,000 units. The decline reflected the discontinuation of F-150 Lightning and production adjustments for Mustang Mach-E.

The segment reported an EBIT loss of $1.06 billion, narrowing from $1.41 billion a year earlier. However, its EBIT margin deteriorated to negative 86.5% from negative 79.1%, reflecting reduced revenues and continued investments in next-generation products.

Management expects to launch the affordable electric vehicle, Fathom, in the fourth quarter of 2027, with a starting price below $30,000. Ford Energy also remains on track to establish 20 gigawatt-hours of annual battery capacity by the end of 2027.

Many investors own Tesla (NASDAQ: TSLA) shares because they believe in the potential of future product platforms like the Cybercab autonomous robotaxi, and the Optimus humanoid robot. But over 70% of the company's revenue still comes from selling passenger electric vehicles (EVs), and this business continues to struggle under the weight of significant global competition.

Tesla's EV deliveries grew in the first half of 2026, after declining for two-straight years. But they took another step backwards in the third quarter (ended Sept. 30), dragging down the company's revenue and earnings.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Tesla stock is down 20% from last year's record high as I write this on Oct. 26, but should investors buy the dip, or is more downside to come? Read on for the surprising answer.

Image source: Tesla.
Tesla's earnings just turned lower yet again

Tesla delivered 838,149 EVs during the first half of 2026, an increase of 16% from the same period last year. The company then delivered a further 486,532 EVs in the third quarter, and although it blew away Wall Street's average forecast of 461,974, it represented a year-over-year decline of 2%.

Tesla has struggled to grow its EV sales consistently amid the increasingly competitive global landscape, particularly with low-cost Chinese manufacturers flooding key markets like Europe. Brands like BYD and Geely sell EVs at much lower starting price points than Tesla, while offering many of the same features. Tesla actually cut prices during the third quarter to bolster sales, and yet its deliveries still declined.

The combination of falling sales and lower prices is weighing on the company's bottom line, contributing to a 44% decline in its generally accepted accounting principles (GAAP) earnings per share during the third quarter alone. Its trailing 12-month earnings have now declined by 79% over the last two years to just $0.91 per share. This has significant implications for Tesla's valuation, which I'll discuss further in a moment.

TSLA EPS Diluted (TTM) data by YCharts

Rather than compete in a race to the bottom on price, Tesla chief executive Elon Musk is pulling Tesla back from the passenger EV business instead. He withdrew the premium Model S and Model X vehicles from the lineup earlier this year, and allocated the production capacity to the Optimus humanoid robot instead -- a product he says won't be ready to sell to customers until the end of 2027.
